title: Great Red Spot
wiki_lead: The Great Red Spot is a persistent, elliptical high-pressure region in the atmosphere of the planet Jupiter, producing the largest anticyclonic storm in the Solar System. It is the most recognizable feature on Jupiter owing to its red-orange color, whose origin is due to a sunburn effect, in which high-altitude chemical compounds are blasted by solar radiation. Located 22 degrees south of Jupiter's equator, it produces wind speeds up to 496 km/h (308 mph). It was first observed in September 1831, with 60 recorded observations between then and 1878, when continuous observations began. A similar spot was observed from 1665 to 1713; if this is the same storm, it has existed for at least 361 years, but a study from 2024 suggested this is not the case.

The Great Red Spot is a persistent, elliptical high-pressure region in the atmosphere of the planet Jupiter, producing the largest anticyclonic storm in the Solar System. It is the most recognizable feature on Jupiter owing to its red-orange color, whose origin is due to a sunburn effect, in which high-altitude chemical compounds are blasted by solar radiation. Located 22 degrees south of Jupiter's equator, it produces wind speeds up to 496 km/h (308 mph). It was first observed in September 1831, with 60 recorded observations between then and 1878, when continuous observations began. A similar spot was observed from 1665 to 1713; if this is the same storm, it has existed for at least 361 years, but a study from 2024 suggested this is not the case.


Observation history


First observations

The Great Red Spot may have existed before 1664, but it could be that the present spot was first seen only in 1830, and was well studied only after a prominent appearance in 1879. The storm that was seen in the 17th century may have been different from the storm that exists today. A long gap separates its period of current study after 1830 from the 17th century discovery. It is unknown whether the original spot dissipated and reformed, whether it faded away, or whether observers between the late 17th century and early 19th century simply failed to study and record it.
The first sighting of the Great Red Spot is often credited to Robert Hooke, who described a spot on the planet in May 1664. However, it is likely that Hooke's spot was not only in another belt altogether (the North Equatorial Belt, as opposed to the current Great Red Spot in the South Equatorial Belt), but also that it was in the shadow of a transiting moon, most likely Callisto. In the following year, Giovanni Cassini describes "a permanent [spot] which was often seen to return in the same place with the same size and shape", calculating its rotation period to be 9 h 56 min. With fluctuations in visibility, Cassini's spot was observed from 1665 to 1713, but the 48-year observational gap makes the identity of the two spots inconclusive. Because of the older spot's shorter observational history and slower motion than the modern spot, it is difficult to conclude that they are the same.
A minor mystery concerns a Jovian spot depicted in a 1711 canvas by Donato Creti, which is exhibited in the Vatican. It is part of a series of panels in which different (magnified) heavenly bodies serve as backdrops for various Italian scenes, all overseen by the astronomer Eustachio Manfredi for accuracy, Creti's painting is the first known depiction of a large spot on Jupiter as red (albeit raised to the Jovian northern hemisphere due to an optical inversion inherent to the era's telescopes). No Jovian feature was explicitly described in writing as red before the late 19th century.

grok_lead: The Great Red Spot is a persistent anticyclonic storm in the southern hemisphere of Jupiter, characterized by its massive scale, reddish hue, and counterclockwise rotation around a high-pressure center, trapped between two powerful jet streams in the planet's turbulent atmosphere. This enormous weather system, the largest and longest-lasting storm known in the Solar System, has been continuously observed for over 190 years since around 1831, though earlier similar spots were noted in the 17th century, with recent analysis debating if it is the same feature; winds reach speeds of up to 425 miles per hour (684 kilometers per hour). The Great Red Spot has endured as a dynamic feature amid Jupiter's banded cloud layers of ammonia and water suspended in hydrogen and helium. Its reddish coloration likely arises from complex chemical reactions, such as the breakdown of simple molecules by ultraviolet sunlight or interactions involving ammonium hydrosulfide with cosmic rays, creating a chromophore that absorbs blue light and scatters red wavelengths. Historically spanning up to 25,500 miles (41,000 kilometers) in widthânearly three times Earth's diameter âthe storm has been shrinking steadily, measuring about 10,250 miles (16,500 kilometers) across as of 2024, the smallest size recorded, while extending roughly 200 to 500 km (120 to 310 miles) deep into Jupiter's atmosphere. Lacking a solid surface, the storm's structure allows it to persist without friction, warmer at its core than surrounding cooler clouds, as revealed by infrared observations. Recent spacecraft missions, including NASA's Juno probe flybys since 2016 and Hubble Space Telescope monitoring through 2024, have shown the Great Red Spot oscillating in shape and speed over 90-day cycles, behaving like a deformable " stress ball " while continuing to shrink, providing insights into Jupiter's atmospheric dynamics and storm longevity.
